problem: Static scene graph representations used for embodied navigation ignore that movable objects change which regions are passable, so agents fail when paths are blocked in rearranged scenes.
motivation: Realistic indoor environments contain movable objects (chairs, boxes) whose states alter navigability. Modeling passability conditioned on object state and interaction feedback should reduce blocked-path failures and improve efficiency.
key_idea: Train a neural graph encoder to predict passability relations between spatial regions conditioned on object states from RGB-D observations and interaction feedback, yielding a traversable scene structure that accounts for object mobility.
insight: Only the abstract was available, so no ablations can be cited. The claimed gain over static scene graphs (28.4% fewer blocked-path failures, 16.7% better efficiency) suggests that conditioning edge passability on object state and interaction feedback is what matters.
method: Neural graph encoder: predicts passability relations between spatial regions in a scene graph, conditioned on object states.
Inputs: RGB-D observations plus interaction feedback (outcomes of interacting with or pushing objects).
Training data: 15,000 simulated navigation trajectories in rearranged indoor scenes.
Downstream use: the learned traversable structure guides navigation, compared against static scene graph baselines.

setting.backbone: neural graph encoder (details not given in abstract)
setting.training_data: 15,000 simulated navigation trajectories in rearranged indoor scenes

results: Per the abstract, the learned scene structure reduces navigation failures due to blocked paths by 28.4% and improves average navigation efficiency by 16.7% versus static scene graph representations. No absolute numbers or benchmarks were available.
